summary: Meningitis is a severe infection of the meninges, the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It presents with fever, severe headache, and stiff neck, and can lead to rapid deterioration and serious complications.

sections.p: Meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges, typically caused by infection. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion supported by investigations, especially lumbar puncture, to identify the causative agent and inflammatory markers.
b: Key signs include fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status.
In infants, irritability, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle may be present.

sections.p: Meningitis can range from mild to life-threatening. Severity is often assessed by the patient's clinical status, vital signs, and neurological examination, with rapid deterioration possible.
b: Rapid assessment of consciousness and haemodynamic stability is crucial.
Complications can significantly impact the patient's outcome and long-term prognosis.

sections.p: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency. Viral meningitis is more common but usually less severe. Other causes include fungal, parasitic, and non-infectious inflammatory conditions.
b: Bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae.
Tuberculous meningitis: common in low-resource settings.
Viral: Enteroviruses, Herpes Simplex Virus.
Fungal: Cryptococcus (especially in immunocompromised individuals).

sections.p: Common symptoms include sudden onset of high fever, severe headache, photophobia, and a stiff neck. Altered mental status, from confusion to coma, can also occur. Seizures are a frequent complication.
b: Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity) is a hallmark sign.
Photophobia (sensitivity to light) is common.
Altered mental status can range from mild confusion to coma.

sections.p: Lumbar puncture is essential for diagnosis, analysing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for cells, protein, glucose, and Gram stain/culture. Blood tests and imaging may also be needed.

t.b: To identify the causative organism and inflammatory markers in CSF. Elevated white blood cells, protein, and low glucose suggest bacterial meningitis. Normal or slightly elevated cells and protein suggest viral meningitis. Culture confirms the specific pathogen.
To detect bacteraemia, which can indicate the source of infection or spread. Positive cultures help identify the pathogen and guide antibiotic choice.
To assess for signs of infection (e.g., elevated white blood cell count).
To rule out complications like brain abscess, hydrocephalus, or mass effect, especially if there are focal neurological signs or if lumbar puncture is contraindicated.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid deterioration of consciousness, seizures, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Complications are serious and can be permanent.
b: Seizures
Cerebral edema and herniation
Cranial nerve palsies
Hearing loss
Hydrocephalus
Neurological deficits (e.g., weakness, cognitive impairment)

sections.p: Prompt antibiotic therapy is critical for bacterial meningitis. Supportive care includes fluid management, fever control, and seizure management. Specific treatment targets the underlying cause.
b: Empirical antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) should be started immediately if bacterial meningitis is suspected.
Corticosteroids may be used to reduce inflammation and neurological sequelae.
Supportive care includes monitoring vital signs, managing seizures, and maintaining fluid balance.

sections.p: Follow-up is essential to monitor for complications and long-term sequelae. Prevention strategies include vaccination and prompt treatment of underlying infections.
b: Vaccination against common bacterial pathogens (e.g., Pneumococcus, Meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b) is key.
Prophylactic antibiotics may be given to close contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis.
Early recognition and treatment of infections can prevent secondary meningitis.

sections.p: Several conditions can mimic meningitis, requiring careful differentiation based on clinical presentation and investigations.
b: Encephalitis
Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Brain abscess
Migraine
Cervical spine pathology

sections.p: Lumbar puncture results can be normal in early or partially treated meningitis. Imaging may be normal in early stages or if the pathology is subtle.
b: A normal white blood cell count in CSF does not exclude meningitis, especially in immunocompromised patients.
Fever may be absent in some cases, particularly in the very young or elderly.
Focal neurological signs can be absent despite significant intracranial pathology.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of meningitis?
faq.a: Bacterial meningitis is the most dangerous, with common causes including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Viral meningitis is more frequent but usually less severe.
Yes, vaccination against key bacterial pathogens like Pneumococcus, Meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b significantly reduces the risk.

faq.q: What are the long-term effects of meningitis?
faq.a: Long-term effects can include hearing loss, learning disabilities, developmental delays, and neurological deficits, depending on the severity and cause of the infection.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A systematic history and focused exam are essential to raise suspicion of meningitis and rule out mimics. In low‑resource settings, the same principles apply, but clinicians must be alert to local epidemiology and comorbidities.
b: History:
• Onset, duration and character of headache (sudden, throbbing, diffuse).
• Fever pattern (high, persistent).
• Neck pain or stiffness, difficulty turning head.
• Photophobia, nausea/vomiting.
• Altered mental status (confusion, lethargy, seizures).
• Recent infections (upper respiratory, ear, sinus).
• Travel, exposure to sick contacts, vaccination status.
• HIV status, TB exposure, immunosuppression, malnutrition, pregnancy.
• In infants: poor feeding, irritability, bulging fontanelle, seizures.

t.b: Elicited by passive neck flexion; a positive result suggests meningeal irritation.
Passive hip flexion causes neck flexion; positive indicates meningeal irritation.
Passive knee extension with hip flexed causes pain; positive suggests meningitis.
Assesses consciousness; lower scores predict worse outcome.
Unequal or sluggish pupils may indicate raised intracranial pressure.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Rapid, accurate investigations guide diagnosis, severity assessment and treatment. In resource‑limited settings, prioritise the most informative tests and use clinical judgment when tests are unavailable.
b: Lumbar puncture (LP) CSF analysis – first line for diagnosis.
• Cell count: neutrophil predominance suggests bacterial; lymphocyte suggests viral or TB.
• Protein: >0.8 g/L bacterial; <0.5 g/L viral.
• Glucose: <2.2 mmol/L or <40% serum indicates bacterial; normal in viral.
• Gram stain & culture: identifies organism; sensitivity 50‑70% bacterial.
• PCR (if available): rapid detection of viral or TB DNA.

t.b: >1000/µL strongly suggests bacterial meningitis; 100‑500/µL is equivocal.

Positive in 30‑50% bacterial meningitis; guides antibiotic choice.

Elevated in bacterial; helps differentiate from viral.

sections.p: Classification of meningitis informs prognosis and management. Severity is graded by clinical status and CSF findings, with specific thresholds guiding escalation.
b: Bacterial meningitis – diagnosis confirmed by CSF neutrophilia, low glucose, high protein, positive culture or PCR.
• Viral meningitis – CSF lymphocytosis, normal glucose, normal protein, negative bacterial culture.
• TB meningitis – CSF lymphocytes, low glucose, high protein, positive AFB or PCR; often chronic course.

t.b: Score ≥4 predicts high mortality; includes altered consciousness, seizures, hypotension, high CSF neutrophils.
≤8 indicates severe disease; requires ICU care.
>250 mmH₂O = raised ICP; >350 mmH₂O = urgent decompression.
>1000/µL = bacterial; 100‑500/µL = equivocal.
>0.8 g/L bacterial; <0.5 g/L viral.
<2.2 mmol/L bacterial; >2.2 mmol/L normal.

sections.p: Several conditions mimic meningitis; distinguishing features rely on history, exam and targeted investigations.
b: Neuro‑cysticercosis – chronic headache, seizures; CSF normal or eosinophilic; neuroimaging shows cysts.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage – sudden severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness; CT shows blood.
Intracranial mass with raised ICP – focal deficits, papilledema; imaging required.
Drug‑induced aseptic meningitis – recent NSAID or antibiotics; CSF sterile.
Traumatic LP – blood in CSF; repeat LP after 24 h to confirm.

sections.p: A structured approach ensures rapid control of infection, prevention of neurologic injury, and safe escalation if the patient deteriorates.
b: 1. Immediate ABCs – secure airway, give high‑flow oxygen, obtain large‑bore IV, start isotonic fluids; obtain blood cultures before antibiotics.
2. Empiric antibiotics – ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) plus vancomycin for all ages; add ampicillin for infants, the elderly, or immunocompromised to cover Listeria.
3. Adjunctive dexamethasone – give with the first dose of antibiotics; taper after 4 days only if pneumococcal meningitis is confirmed, otherwise stop with antibiotics.
4. Monitor – neurological status (GCS), pupil size, ICP signs, vitals, urine output, and serum electrolytes every hour initially.

5. Escalate – if GCS falls >2 points, new focal deficit, or refractory hypotension, obtain emergent CT, consider neurosurgical drainage, start vasopressors, and arrange transfer to a centre with intensive care and neurosurgery.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse effects early prevents secondary injury and guides safe continuation of therapy.
b: Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime – risk of biliary sludging and allergic rash; if jaundice or cholestasis appears, switch to a non‑beta‑lactam such as meropenem.
Vancomycin – nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; monitor serum creatinine and hearing; if creatinine rises >0.5 mg/dL, reduce dose or change to linezolid.
Ampicillin – possible hypersensitivity; if rash or anaphylaxis occurs, replace with meropenem and add Listeria‑active coverage later if needed.
Dexamethasone – hyperglycaemia, GI bleeding; check blood glucose every 4 h, give proton‑pump inhibitor in diabetics or ulcer history.
Gentamicin (neonates) – ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; obtain baseline renal function and auditory screening, adjust interval if creatinine rises.

sections.p: Complications often develop within the first 48 h; early detection triggers escalation to intensive care or neurosurgery.
b: Seizure – treat with a loading dose of a short‑acting benzodiazepine; if recurrent, start a maintenance antiepileptic and consider EEG.
Raised intracranial pressure – assess papilledema, Cushing’s triad; if signs present, obtain urgent CT, start mannitol or hypertonic saline, and arrange ventriculostomy.
Cerebral infarction/vasculitis – new focal deficit; repeat imaging, consider adding high‑dose steroids if vasculitis suspected.
Hearing loss – perform bedside otoacoustic emission testing when possible; refer to audiology for early rehabilitation.
Hydrocephalus – progressive head‑ache, vomiting, decreasing GCS; neurosurgical shunt placement is indicated.

sections.p: These conditions modify presentation, CSF interpretation, and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV (CD4 < 100 cells/µL) – high risk of cryptococcal meningitis; CSF India‑ink positive, low glucose; add amphotericin B plus flucytosine, avoid steroids unless bacterial co‑infection proven.
Tuberculosis – CSF lymphocytic, protein > 100 mg/dL, glucose < 40 % of serum; start empiric anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) before culture confirmation.
Pregnancy – ceftriaxone and ampicillin are safe; avoid tetracyclines; monitor fetal heart rate and give antenatal steroids if pre‑term delivery likely.
Diabetes – hyperglycaemia worsened by dexamethasone; check glucose hourly, start insulin infusion if >180 mg/dL.
Renal failure – adjust vancomycin and gentamicin dosing; avoid nephrotoxic agents if creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min.
Liver failure – limit rifampicin dose; use ethambutol and streptomycin if TB suspected; monitor transaminases with all hepatotoxic drugs.

sections.p: Tailored strategies address the unique physiology and epidemiology of each population.
b: Children (<5 y) – cefotaxime plus vancomycin; add ampicillin for Listeria in infants <1 month; monitor for otitis media as source; vaccinate against Hib, PCV, and meningococcus where available.
Pregnant women – ceftriaxone plus ampicillin; give dexamethasone only if pneumococcal confirmed; fetal monitoring with continuous cardiotocography.
Elderly (>65 y) – ceftriaxone plus vancomycin plus ampicillin for Listeria; watch for atypical presentations (confusion, falls); adjust fluids for cardiac reserve.
People with HIV – early cryptococcal antigen testing; if positive, start amphotericin B plus flucytosine; continue antiretroviral therapy after 4‑6 weeks of induction.
Low‑resource settings – if LP cannot be performed safely, give empiric ceftriaxone plus vancomycin; use bedside Gram stain; arrange referral for CT if focal signs.

facts: In suspected TB meningitis, start empiric RIPE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) after CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein; adjust once culture available.
In HIV pts with CD4 < 100 cells/µL, high risk for cryptococcal meningitis; perform India ink and cryptococcal antigen early.
Severe headache, fever >38 °C, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, altered mental status are key clinical features.
Lumbar puncture CSF: opening pressure >20 cmH₂O indicates raised ICP; glucose <40 mg/dL, protein >100 mg/dL, neutrophil >1000/µL suggest bacterial meningitis.
In infants, bulging fontanelle, irritability, poor feeding are red flags; in adults, seizures, focal deficits, papilledema are critical.
In malnutrition, consider higher antibiotic doses due to altered pharmacokinetics; monitor electrolytes closely.

vivas.q: What are the key clinical features that would lead you to suspect meningitis?
vivas.a: Fever >38 °C, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, altered mental status; in infants, bulging fontanelle, irritability, poor feeding.

vivas.q: What is the first investigation you would order for a suspected bacterial meningitis?
vivas.a: Urgent lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement; if contraindicated, obtain CT head first.

vivas.q: Why is dexamethasone started before antibiotics in bacterial meningitis?
vivas.a: It reduces inflammatory damage and improves survival, especially in pneumococcal disease.

vivas.q: When should you stop ampicillin in a child <5 yrs receiving cefotaxime and vancomycin?
vivas.a: Stop once CSF shows no Listeria (negative Gram stain, culture) and age >1 yr.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a CSF opening pressure >20 cmH₂O?
vivas.a: Indicates raised intracranial pressure; requires therapeutic CSF drainage or osmotherapy.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate bacterial from viral meningitis on CSF?
vivas.a: Bacterial: neutrophil >1000/µL, glucose <40 mg/dL, protein >100 mg/dL; viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose, protein 50–100 mg/dL.

vivas.q: Why is gentamicin avoided in neonates?
vivas.a: Neonates have immature renal function; gentamicin toxicity risk is high, so use ampicillin plus gentamicin with careful monitoring.

vivas.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of meningitis beyond the neonatal period?
Which organism is most typical of a shunt-associated infection?
What is the key histological finding in cerebral vessels during bacterial meningitis?
vivas.a: Perivascular neutrophilic infiltrates with vasculitis; fibrinoid necrosis is not typical.

vivas.q: Which underlying host condition places a child at 20‑ to 100‑fold higher risk of pneumococcal meningitis?
In which geographic region does serogroup A Neisseria meningitidis account for 80‑85% of epidemic outbreaks?
What is the impact of vaccination on Hib meningitis incidence?
vivas.a: Hib vaccination has reduced Hib meningitis by >95% in vaccinated populations.

vivas.q: Describe the management of raised intracranial pressure in meningitis.
vivas.a: Therapeutic lumbar puncture, osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline, head elevation, and avoid steroids unless indicated.

vivas.q: Why is empiric anti‑TB therapy started before definitive results?
vivas.a: Because TB meningitis progresses slowly; early treatment improves outcomes; therapy is guided by clinical suspicion and CSF findings.

mcqs.q: A 3‑year‑old presents with fever, stiff neck, and seizures. CSF shows neutrophils 1200/µL, glucose 30 mg/dL, protein 150 mg/dL. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
mcqs.e: Pneumococcal meningitis requires ceftriaxone plus vancomycin; ampicillin is not needed in this age group.

mcqs.q: An HIV‑positive adult with CD4 90 cells/µL has headache and fever. CSF shows 200 cells/µL, 10% lymphocytes, India ink positive. What is the most likely pathogen?
mcqs.e: India ink positivity indicates cryptococcal infection.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a red flag for bacterial meningitis?
mcqs.e: Chronic cough is not a red flag for meningitis.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a hallmark histological finding in bacterial meningitis?
mcqs.e: Perivascular neutrophilic infiltrates with vasculitis are typical.

mistakes: Adding ampicillin to all adult regimens without considering age or Listeria risk.
Stopping dexamethasone after 4 days regardless of organism confirmation.
Initiating high‑dose rifampicin in liver failure without dose adjustment.
Using gentamicin in neonates without monitoring serum levels.
Ignoring the need for imaging before LP in suspected raised ICP.
Overlooking HIV CD4 < 100 cells/µL as high risk for cryptococcal meningitis.
Failing to reassess for other shock causes if hypotension persists after fluids.
Assuming all bacterial meningitis cases are pneumococcal without CSF confirmation.
